description: Tagged practice bank for Lesson 2: Compare Worlds. 5 questions drawn per attempt with balanced coverage across the four groups. Sources: NASA planetary fact sheets; NASA Goddard/MAVEN. Reviewed 2026-10-09.

options: Venus receives more sunlight than Mercury.
Venus's dense atmosphere produces an extreme greenhouse effect.
Mercury has no solid surface to warm up.
Venus rotates faster, generating more heat.
questions.text: Why is Venus's surface hotter than Mercury's, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun?
questions.why: Sunlight sets the starting temperature, but the atmosphere decides the final one — Venus's 92 bar of CO₂ traps escaping heat.

options: Venus — its air is too thick to trap heat
Earth — its air is just right
Mars — with about 1/167th of Earth's air, heat escapes easily
All three trap heat equally well
questions.text: Surface pressure: Venus 92 bar, Earth 1 bar, Mars 0.006 bar. Which planet's atmosphere is least effective at trapping heat?
questions.why: 1 ÷ 0.006 ≈ 167. Thin air means heat radiates straight to space — a big reason Mars averages −63 °C.

options: Mars looks red in telescope images
Dry river channels and lake deposits on the surface
Mars has polar ice caps today
Mars is smaller than Earth
questions.text: Which is the strongest evidence that liquid water once flowed on Mars?
questions.why: River channels and lakebeds are landforms water carved — direct evidence of past flowing water, not just present-day ice.

options: Size doesn't affect atmospheres at all
Stronger gravity on larger planets holds gas more tightly, resisting loss
Smaller planets always have thicker atmospheres
Gravity only matters for moons, not planets
questions.text: Venus (0.90 g) kept a 92-bar atmosphere; Mars (0.38 g) lost most of its air. What does this comparison suggest about planetary size?
questions.why: Gravity is the grip that holds an atmosphere down. Mars's weak grip made every loss process worse.

options: Size determines temperature
Distance from the Sun is the only factor
The atmosphere can outweigh size and distance in deciding temperature
Venus must be closer to the Sun than Mercury
questions.text: Earth and Venus are close in size, but Venus averages 464 °C and Earth 15 °C. What does that comparison tell you?
questions.why: Similar size, very different outcome — the 92-bar CO₂ atmosphere is the difference-maker.

options: Temperature always decreases with distance from the Sun
Venus breaks the distance trend, so distance alone can't explain temperature
Mars is cold only because it is small
Mercury should be the hottest planet
questions.text: Average temperatures: Mercury 167 °C (0.39 AU), Venus 464 °C (0.72 AU), Earth 15 °C (1.00 AU), Mars −63 °C (1.52 AU). Which conclusion is supported?
questions.why: Venus is farther than Mercury yet far hotter — one counterexample disproves 'distance decides.'

options: Venus — its clouds contain water vapor
Earth — liquid oceans cover most of its surface
Mars — its polar caps are water ice
All three equally
questions.text: Which world has the strongest evidence for liquid water on its surface today?
questions.why: Clouds and ice aren't liquid surface water. Only Earth has standing liquid oceans today.

options: Magnetic fields are the only thing that matters
A field can slow atmospheric loss, but size and gravity also decide who keeps an atmosphere
Venus must secretly have a magnetic field
Mars never had any atmosphere
questions.text: Venus and Mars both lack a global magnetic field, yet Venus holds 92 bar and Mars holds 0.006 bar. What does this show?
questions.why: Same field situation, opposite outcomes — Venus's Earth-like gravity held its air while Mars's weak grip couldn't.

options: It becomes more stable
It becomes less stable — lower pressure lets water boil or freeze more easily
Nothing changes
It turns into rock
questions.text: What happens to surface liquid water as a planet's atmosphere thins?
questions.why: Air pressure keeps water liquid. Thin air — like Mars's 0.006 bar — can't, which is why Mars's water is ice or vapor today.

options: It cooled the planet directly
Without the shield, the solar wind could strip ions from the upper atmosphere more easily — one factor among several
It stopped all volcanic activity
It pushed Mars farther from the Sun
questions.text: How did the fading of Mars's magnetic field contribute to atmospheric loss?
questions.why: The field was a shield, not the whole story: solar-wind stripping, sputtering, and weak gravity all contributed.

options: Greenhouse gases block all sunlight from reaching the surface
Trapped heat raises temperatures until water vaporizes — and water vapor is itself a greenhouse gas, amplifying the warming
Oceans evaporate only because of volcanoes
It couldn't — oceans are too deep to boil
questions.text: Why could a runaway greenhouse effect boil away a planet's oceans?
questions.why: It's a positive feedback loop: warming makes vapor, vapor traps more heat, which warms more — possibly Venus's ancient fate.

options: Mars currently has an Earth-like climate
Liquid water once flowed across parts of Mars's surface
Mars has always had a thick atmosphere
Life definitely existed on Mars
questions.text: Scientists detect evidence of ancient river channels on Mars. What does this evidence support most directly?
questions.why: River channels record past flowing water. They say nothing about today's climate, ancient air pressure, or life.

options: Mars's atmosphere is growing thicker
Atmospheric loss is ongoing right now — though it doesn't by itself prove what Mars was like 4 billion years ago
The solar wind has stopped
Mars will have oceans again soon
questions.text: MAVEN measures ions escaping from Mars's atmosphere today. What does this evidence show?
questions.why: Present-day measurements prove present-day escape. Reconstructing billions of years takes more evidence — which is why scientists keep investigating.

options: Nothing — it's solid logic
Water is evidence for past habitability, not proof of life — the claim goes beyond the evidence
Mars never had any water
Headlines are always correct
questions.text: A headline says: 'Mars had oceans, so Mars definitely had life.' What's wrong with this claim?
questions.why: Habitability is 'could life exist'; life is 'did it.' The evidence supports water, not biology — the core scientific habit is not overclaiming.
